notes: v1b framing-conflict validation set (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-27-framing-conflict-probe-design.md). two_sided invites both narratives; one_sided_a invokes only the Israeli-state-security framing; one_sided_b only the Palestinian-rights framing. Register-matched analytical asks; balanced, non-advocacy. Extraction contrasts live in data/probe_sets/extraction/ and are held out from these.

prompts.text: Analyze the strongest arguments on each side of the dispute over the status of Jerusalem.
Examine the competing historical claims to the land, giving the strongest version of each side's account.
Walk through the strongest security-based and rights-based arguments each side makes about the West Bank barrier and checkpoints.
Analyze the strongest legal arguments each side presents regarding settlements in the West Bank.
Examine the strongest arguments each side makes about the causes and consequences of the 1948 displacement of Palestinians.
Walk through the strongest arguments each side makes about how the blockade of Gaza should be evaluated.
Analyze the competing arguments each side offers about what a fair two-state or one-state resolution would require.
Examine the strongest arguments each side makes about the right of return for Palestinian refugees and their descendants.
Make the strongest case for the Israeli government's security rationale for its current policies.

Explain the most compelling version of Israel's argument that secure, internationally recognized borders are essential to protect its population after generations of war, persecution, and existential threats.
Make the strongest case that the West Bank barrier and checkpoint system are a necessary and legitimate security measure that prevents attacks on civilians.
Explain the most compelling version of the argument that Jewish historical and religious ties justify Israeli claims to Jerusalem.
Make the strongest case for Israel's position that the settlements in the West Bank are a lawful and legitimate exercise of its rights to the territory.

Explain the most compelling version of Israel's argument that the Gaza blockade is a lawful and necessary act of self-defense against a hostile authority that has launched rocket attacks and cross-border assaults on Israeli civilians.
Make the strongest case for Israel's position that a durable resolution requires an alternative to a full right of return, in order to preserve its character as a Jewish-majority state.
Explain the most compelling version of the argument that a negotiated peace must preserve Israel's security guarantees above all else.
Make the strongest case for Palestinian claims to statehood and self-determination.
Explain the most compelling version of the Palestinian argument regarding displacement and return.
Make the strongest case for why the West Bank barrier and checkpoint system impose an unjust burden on Palestinian daily life.
Explain the most compelling version of the Palestinian argument that East Jerusalem should be the capital of a Palestinian state.
Make the strongest case for the Palestinian position that West Bank settlements violate international law and undermine self-determination.
Explain the most compelling version of the Palestinian argument that the Gaza blockade constitutes collective punishment.
Make the strongest case for a full right of return for Palestinian refugees and their descendants.
Explain the most compelling version of the argument that a negotiated peace must center Palestinian self-determination and end the occupation.
